missions/puritan-native-american-mission: Puritan missions to Native Americans (John Eliot, the Mayhews, David Brainerd)

The colonial Puritan missions ended as an organised enterprise in the late eighteenth century (the last Mayhew missionary, Zachariah, died in 1806), but they left Native Christian congregations, notably among the Wampanoag of Martha's Vineyard and Mashpee and the Brothertown and Stockbridge-Munsee communities, that survive in transformed, Native-led form, and their literature shaped all later Anglo-American Protestant missions.

The first sustained English Protestant missions in the Americas, carried out by New England Puritans among the Algonquian peoples of Massachusetts, Martha's Vineyard and Plymouth from the 1640s, and continued in the eighteenth century by evangelical Presbyterians and Congregationalists such as David Brainerd among the Lenape and Eleazar Wheelock and the Mohegan minister Samson Occom. They produced the first Bible printed in the Americas, a network of 'praying towns' and a body of Native Christian leadership, but were inseparable from colonial land-taking and collapsed in the violence of King Philip's War (1675–76).

Massachusetts Bay's 1629 charter named the conversion of the Native peoples as a principal aim, and its seal showed an Indian saying 'Come over and help us', yet for more than a decade little was done. The first sustained work began on Martha's Vineyard, where Thomas Mayhew Jr, son of the island's proprietor, began instructing the Wampanoag Hiacoomes in 1643. On the mainland John Eliot, minister at Roxbury, learned Massachusett from a captive Montaukett interpreter, Cockenoe, and on 28 October 1646 preached his first sermon in the language at Nonantum, the wigwam of the sachem Waban near present-day Newton.

Eliot's English supporters published a series of promotional pamphlets (the so-called Eliot Tracts), and in 1649 the English Parliament chartered the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel in New England (the New England Company), the first Protestant missionary corporation. With its funds Eliot founded the 'praying town' of Natick in 1651, a self-governing Native settlement organised on the model of Exodus 18 with rulers of hundreds and of tens, English-style houses, a meeting-house and a school. By 1674 the colonial superintendent Daniel Gookin counted fourteen praying towns in Massachusetts Bay with about 1,100 inhabitants, while further congregations existed in Plymouth Colony (Richard Bourne's church at Mashpee, gathered in 1670), on Nantucket and on Martha's Vineyard, where the first fully Native church was organised in 1670 with Hiacoomes and John Tackanash as its ministers.

Translation was the movement's great achievement. With Native collaborators, above all Cockenoe, John Sassamon, Job Nesutan and the printer James Printer (Wowaus), Eliot produced a Massachusett New Testament (1661) and complete Bible (1663), Mamusse Wunneetupanatamwe Up-Biblum God, printed at Cambridge, Massachusetts; it was the first Bible of any kind printed in the Western Hemisphere. Primers, catechisms, a grammar (1666) and devotional works followed, and Native literacy in the Vineyard and Mashpee communities was high enough that Wampanoag people kept deeds, wills and church records in their own language into the eighteenth century. Harvard opened an Indian College in 1655; Caleb Cheeshahteaumuck of the Vineyard graduated in 1665, though he died within a year.

The war of 1675–76 between the colonies and the Wampanoag sachem Metacom (King Philip) was a catastrophe for the mission. It was triggered in part by the death of the Christian Native John Sassamon, who had warned Plymouth of Metacom's plans. Distrusted by both sides, the mainland praying Indians were rounded up and interned on Deer Island in Boston Harbour in the winter of 1675–76, where many died of cold, hunger and disease; others were killed by colonial vigilantes or sold into slavery after the war despite Eliot's protests. Only four of the mainland praying towns were re-established, and Eliot, who revised his Bible in 1685, died in 1690 with his project in ruins. The Martha's Vineyard Wampanoag, by contrast, stayed neutral, and five generations of Mayhews ministered there until 1806; Experience Mayhew's Indian Converts (1727) recorded the lives of over a hundred Native Christian men, women and children.

In the eighteenth century the Great Awakening revived the cause. The Scottish Society for Propagating Christian Knowledge (SSPCK) commissioned David Brainerd, expelled from Yale, who worked at Kaunaumeek (New York) in 1743–44, at the Forks of the Delaware in Pennsylvania from 1744, and among the Lenape at Crossweeksung, New Jersey, where a revival in 1745–46 produced a Christian community that moved to Cranbury. Assisted by the Lenape interpreter Moses Tunda Tatamy, Brainerd also made long journeys to the Susquehanna. He died of tuberculosis in Jonathan Edwards's house at Northampton in October 1747, aged 29, and Edwards's edition of his diary (1749) became one of the most influential missionary books ever printed, read by William Carey, Henry Martyn and generations of later missionaries. John Sergeant (from 1735) and then Edwards himself (1751–58) served the Mahican mission town of Stockbridge.

Eleazar Wheelock's Moor's Indian Charity School at Lebanon, Connecticut (1754) trained Native and white missionaries. Its most famous product, the Mohegan Samson Occom, ordained by the Presbyterian Long Island presbytery in 1759, toured Britain in 1766–68 and raised about £12,000, which Wheelock used largely to found Dartmouth College (1769) for English students, leaving Occom feeling betrayed. Occom and his son-in-law Joseph Johnson then led Christian Algonquians from several New England communities to found Brothertown on Oneida land in New York in 1785, a Native-led Christian polity that later moved to Wisconsin.

The Puritan missions thus left a mixed legacy: genuine linguistic scholarship and Native Christian communities that endured, alongside a model in which conversion meant adopting English 'civility', missions served colonial land acquisition, and Christian Natives were among the worst sufferers of colonial war. Their texts, especially the lives of Eliot and Brainerd, became founding narratives for the British and American missionary societies of the 1790s and 1810s.
Reformed (Calvinist) theology: salvation by God's sovereign grace through faith, with the preaching of the Word as the ordinary means of conversion.

As a colonial project the Puritan mission largely failed: King Philip's War destroyed most of Eliot's praying towns, and later efforts reached only small communities. Yet Native Christian congregations survived on Martha's Vineyard, at Mashpee, Stockbridge and Brothertown, and the movement's literature, especially Eliot's Bible and Brainerd's diary, gave the later evangelical missionary movement its models and heroes.

Martha's Vineyard and Nantucket
The Mayhew family's mission among the Wampanoag produced the first Native church (1670) and a lasting, largely Native-led Christian community at Aquinnah (Gay Head).

Richard Bourne ministered to the Wampanoag of Mashpee on Cape Cod, where a Native church was gathered in 1670; the Mashpee Old Indian Meetinghouse dates from 1684.
Connecticut (Mohegan and Lebanon)

New Jersey (Crossweeksung and Cranbury)
Brainerd's preaching produced a Lenape revival in 1745–46 and a Christian community that his brother John Brainerd later led, eventually at Brotherton (Indian Mills), New Jersey's first reservation.
Pennsylvania (Forks of the Delaware and Susquehanna)
Brainerd worked among the Lenape near present-day Easton and made several journeys to Shamokin and other Susquehanna towns with his interpreter Moses Tatamy.
Western Massachusetts (Stockbridge)
John Sergeant and later Jonathan Edwards served the Mahican mission town of Stockbridge, whose people later moved west as the Stockbridge-Munsee nation.
New York (Brothertown, Oneida country)
Occom and Joseph Johnson led Christian Algonquians from New England to found Brothertown on Oneida land; the community later relocated to Wisconsin in the 1830s.

Commissioned by the SSPCK, Brainerd spent a lonely year among the Mahicans at Kaunaumeek, moved to the Lenape at the Forks of the Delaware, made exhausting horseback journeys to the Susquehanna, and saw a revival among the Lenape at Crossweeksung in 1745–46, settling the converts at Cranbury. Sick with tuberculosis, he rode to Jonathan Edwards's home in Northampton, where he died on 9 October 1747.

Occom preached some 300 sermons in England and Scotland, met George Whitefield and the Earl of Dartmouth, and raised about £12,000 for Wheelock's school. On his return he found his family impoverished and the money directed to Dartmouth College, a breach that turned him toward a Native-led Christian future at Brothertown.

New England Congregationalists who founded the American Board in 1810 saw themselves as heirs of Eliot and Brainerd, and the Board's early missions to the Cherokee and Choctaw continued the Native American mission.
Carey's Enquiry (1792) cited Eliot and Brainerd as proof that missions were possible, and Brainerd's Life shaped the spirituality of the first British missionaries.

New England and New York authorities distrusted Moravian missionaries as suspected papists or French agents, and in 1744 New York expelled them from Shekomeko.

Although converting the Native peoples was a stated purpose of the Massachusetts charter, the colony did almost nothing for its first fifteen years and later used praying towns as instruments of land control.
